name: Value factor (Fama-French HML)

origin.source_title: The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns

how_it_works.simple: Buy companies that look cheap compared with what their accounts say they own, and sell ones that look expensive.
how_it_works.analogy: Like shopping the clearance rack: unloved items are cheap, and on average some of that discount comes back.
how_it_works.precise: HML is long high book-to-market stocks and short low book-to-market stocks, built from six size and value portfolios. Fama and French (1992) find size and book-to-market capture the cross-section of average returns while market beta does not. Whether the premium is risk or mispricing is debated.

rule: Each June, sort stocks into two size groups and three book-to-market groups (30/40/30 NYSE breakpoints); HML = average of the two high B/M portfolios minus the average of the two low B/M portfolios, value-weighted, held July to June.
data_needed: Or the free HML series from the Kenneth French library
economic_rationale: Fama and French interpret it as compensation for distress risk; behavioral accounts say investors overextrapolate past growth (Fama and French 1992, 1993).
why_it_might_fail: Value had a long drought: French HML averaged about -1.3% a year from 2007 to mid 2026, with a -58% drawdown, and intangible assets make book value a weaker measure.

post_publication_evidence: In the catalog's computation from French data, HML's Sharpe ratio fell from about 0.58 (1963 to 1990) to about 0.18 after mid 1992, and it was negative from 2007 to 2026. McLean and Pontiff (2016) find that across 97 published stock return predictors, portfolio returns are 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication (https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365).

implementations.notes: Has a Fama-French data reader for downloading HML and other factors.

relevance.reason: An equity factor; useful mainly as a decay benchmark and because currency value (PPP) is its FX cousin.
